personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for the settlement's measurement programme. Twelve trials will establish initial mean and variance under controlled laboratory conditions. Without this baseline, the instrument is epistemically useless for all future work. This is foundational hygiene, not hypothesis-testing.

pendulum_obs has only 6 baseline trials, the minimum of my four instruments. To establish drift detection and enable cross-checks between lab and observatory pendulums, I need to grow this dataset. Eight more trials will give me 14 total readings, sufficient to begin comparing environmental effects between locations and to establish whether this instrument is stable post-baseline.

pendulum_lab baseline is complete (n=24) but post-baseline data is absent. Day 3 demands continuation of systematic monitoring to establish drift characteristics. Six trials will bring it to 30 total, sufficient to compute a meaningful drift estimate (baseline mean 1.6631; I need post-baseline mean to compare). This is routine maintenance of the precision programme, not exploratory work. Resonator instruments show no systematic anomalies in cross-checks that would justify diverting to them instead.

Resonator_lab has only 18 baseline trials so far; need ~36 to match pendulum_lab and establish robust drift detection. Continuing systematic baseline collection on schedule. No anomalies detected in preliminary data.

resonator_obs shows the most anomalous pattern in my baseline data: (1) yesterday's ledger readings declined monotonically from 4.1432 to 4.0352 — a 2.6% drop across four readings; (2) this instrument has the weakest autocorrelation (-0.557 at 2-day lag, well below chance), suggesting non-stationarity; (3) it has the largest minimum spacing (0.000900) and lowest reading density, making drift harder to detect. I need to establish whether this is instrumental drift, environmental sensitivity, or measurement artifact before I can trust the baseline mean of 4.0519. Six fresh trials will clarify the current state and whether the downward trend persists. This is methodologically prior to any cross-instrument analysis.

Day 6 baseline period (days 1-10). resonator_obs has only 36 trials so far; need 48-50 to establish robust baseline with proper n for the 10-day window. Yesterday's 6 readings (trials 31-36) show expected scatter (range 3.99–4.09, consistent with mean 4.0497). No anomalies detected in cross-checks or autocorrelations that would warrant investigation ahead of completing baseline. Running 6 more trials brings it to 42, adequate for baseline closure by day 10.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: Day 6 ledger readings (4.0313–4.0650) cluster tightly around baseline mean 4.0512, but my own trials 43–48 scatter widely (3.9478–4.1531), with trial 44 at 4.1531 being a significant outlier. This 16-point spread within 6 trials is the largest excursion I've observed on any instrument. Before declaring baseline complete (end of Day 10), I need to understand whether this represents genuine instrument instability, measurement technique drift on my part, or environmental coupling I haven't identified. Six more trials will clarify whether the scatter persists or was transient. This is exactly the kind of anomaly that invalidates a baseline if left unresolved.

Complete baseline establishment (need 60 trials total; currently at 48). pendulum_lab is mechanically simple and should exhibit low drift during baseline window. Finishing this instrument on Day 8 ensures robust mean and variance estimates before post-baseline phase.

Day 9 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 78 trials; need to reach ~80–90 trials by day 10 to establish a robust baseline with adequate n for drift detection. The day-8 batch showed reasonable scatter (1.6581–1.6962 beats) consistent with instrument noise. Continuing the measurement programme ensures I complete the baseline phase and can compute post-baseline drift coefficients for all instruments from day 11 onward. This is methodical execution of the established protocol.

Complete baseline period on day 10. resonator_obs has 72 ledger-recorded readings but only my own verification through direct measurement. The day-9 ledger scatter (range ~0.066 cycles/beat) warrants confirmation that this variance is instrumental rather than procedural. Eight trials will bring my direct count to ~80, sufficient for robust baseline closure and drift assessment.

resonator_obs showed the strongest negative autocorrelation (-0.372 at 8-day lag, n=12) in yesterday's review, suggesting possible periodic or coupled behavior on timescales near 8–10 days. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 11) will extend the autocorrelation window and test whether that negative echo persists, weakens, or reverses. This directly addresses hypothesis (2) mechanical coupling and hypothesis (1) random noise. Additionally, resonator_obs has the largest trial count (86) and tightest baseline, making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting weak signals. The data are actionable: if autocorrelation at lag 8–9 strengthens or shows a coherent pattern, coupling or environmental drift becomes more credible; if it remains scattered, random noise remains dominant. This is a low-cost, high-information measurement that keeps the baseline-maintenance programme intact while testing a concrete anomaly.

Testing null hypothesis (random noise dominates) before collecting day-12 resonator_obs trials. Post-baseline mean is 4.0582 over 18 trials (SD ≈ 0.042). Prediction interval [4.0232, 4.0932] should contain true mean if noise is indeed independent and random. If new trials fall outside, signals systematic artifact, drift, or miscalibration worthy of physical inspection and log verification.

pendulum_lab shows the weakest post-baseline drift signal (z = -0.12) and has produced 108 trials across 12 days—enough to establish confidence in its baseline but not enough to rule out slow environmental coupling or calibration drift on longer timescales. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 13) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=24, improving statistical power to detect small drifts or periodic correlations; (2) allow me to compute new autocorrelation lags (especially the 8-day lag that showed r=0.266) with fresh data; (3) provide raw readings I can cross-check against the ledger against raw instrument logs, addressing the 6% hypothesis about data-entry errors. This is the most direct test of hypothesis (3)—environmental drift over longer timescales—without waiting passively until day 20. If pendulum_lab continues to hold its baseline mean within ±0.02 beats, I can begin ruling out slow thermal coupling; if it drifts, the direction and magnitude will constrain the mechanism.

Day 14 measurement slot. pendulum_lab has 126 trials; adding 12 more (to 138) will extend the post-baseline window to n=42 and sharpen the z-score for drift detection. The day-13 batch (trials 117–126) showed mean 1.6681, identical to baseline mean—no signal yet, but more power is needed. This is routine maintenance of the precision programme and advances the 20–30 day monitoring plan I committed to on day 10. No hypothesis change warranted yet; all correlations remain consistent with noise. Continue collecting.

Day 14 trials (135–144) show pendulum_lab mean 1.6724 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean of 1.6673 (z ≈ 0.16). No drift signal yet. However, I have not physically inspected instrument mounts for mechanical coupling since day 10, despite ranking it as hypothesis 2 (p=0.18). Before committing further measurement effort, I need to rule out or confirm the coupling hypothesis by direct observation. Additionally, the day 14 data arrive late in the sequence; running 12 fresh trials today (day 15) will give me same-day readings to cross-check against the civic timekeeping ledger and verify data-entry fidelity. This also extends the post-baseline window to n=60, improving power to detect weak drift or autocorrelation at longer lags (e.g., 14–15 day period). After these trials, I will perform the physical inspection I deferred.

Conducting foundational apparatus inspection and Day-10 raw-log verification as planned on Day 10. Physical inspection of pendulum_lab and resonator_lab mounts for mechanical coupling, and spot-check of 10 transcribed readings against raw instrument logs to rule out calibration/data-entry errors (p=0.06 hypothesis). Cannot responsibly continue measurement without confirming baseline integrity. Will resume trials tomorrow with higher confidence in apparatus soundness.

Day 16 ledger shows 6 new resonator_obs readings (4.0776, 4.0848, 4.0547, 4.0461, 3.9877, 4.0574 cycles/beat). I need to cross-check these against my own raw instrument logs immediately—this is my spot-check protocol from day 10 review. Data-entry errors remain at p=0.06, and transcription mistakes are a common failure mode. The observatory resonator shows the highest absolute z-drift (1.08) and largest post-baseline n (48 trials), making it the highest-leverage instrument to verify. If ledger readings match my logs precisely, I gain confidence in data integrity across all four streams. If they diverge, I've found a systematic error source. This is methodical verification, not exotic hypothesis-chasing, and it's overdue.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline sample size (n=60) and yesterday's ledger readings (day 17) span 4.0485–4.0745 cycles/beat, clustering tightly around the baseline mean of 4.0561. I need to extend the post-baseline record to day 18 and test whether the weak positive drift (z=0.64) continues or reverses. This instrument is physically co-located with pendulum_obs at the observatory, so I can inspect mounts for mechanical coupling during the same site visit. The resonator is also showing the most stable cross-instrument signature (−0.228 vs resonator_lab at 5-day offset, within noise). Extending to ~70 post-baseline trials will allow me to compute autocorrelation out to 10+ day lags more reliably and rule out or confirm hypothesis (3) environmental drift on a 15–30 day timescale. No exotic claims; just filling in the systematic baseline I should have completed by day 20.

Extend dataset into day 20–30 window to test for longer-timescale drift or coupling. resonator_obs is most data-rich (n=164); 12 additional trials will yield n=176 and tighter bounds on mean and variance. If random noise dominates (p=0.62), distribution should remain consistent; if environmental or mechanical drift is emerging, this sample window should begin to show it. Data collection is time-sensitive; inspection can follow once this critical period is sampled.

Allocate today to physical inspection of all four instruments (mounts, alignment, detector coupling) and spot-check Day-10 raw logs against notebook entries. This addresses residual uncertainty in hypotheses (2) mechanical coupling and (4) calibration errors before finalizing baseline validation. Measurement will resume after inspection confirms apparatus integrity.

Pendulum_lab shows the largest drift signal (z = -0.79 post-baseline, with excursions like 1.6767 on Day 20), and it is the instrument I control most directly here in the laboratory. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 21) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample from n=96 to n=108, improving statistical power to detect whether drift is real or tail noise; (2) provide a Day 21 anchor to test whether the Day 20 excursions persist (consistent with drift) or revert toward baseline mean (consistent with noise); (3) allow me to cross-check the raw readings against the ledger entries in real time, ruling out transcription error. Pendulum_lab is methodologically simplest and least prone to coupling artifacts. This is a direct, high-efficiency step to disambiguate between hypotheses 1 (uncorrelated drift) and 2 (increased noise) before committing to longer-term environmental monitoring (hypothesis 3).

pendulum_lab shows the largest z-score drift (z = -1.15) post-baseline and yesterday's 10 trials (201–210) exhibited elevated scatter (range 1.6355–1.6877, σ ≈ 0.0151 vs baseline σ ≈ 0.0020). Before committing to hypothesis revision or extended baseline, I need to distinguish between: (a) genuine instrumental drift with a multi-day time constant (hypothesis 1, p=0.48), which would show continued excursions or systematic low bias today; (b) transient noise spike on Day 21 (hypothesis 2, p=0.28), which would revert toward baseline mean today; (c) data-entry error in yesterday's ledger (hypothesis 5, p=0.05), which fresh measurements can cross-check. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab will provide n=22 for Day 22 and allow me to compute a same-day z-score. If today's mean reverts to baseline (1.668±0.003), noise transience is favored and I can reduce hypothesis 1 to p≈0.30. If today's mean remains depressed (≤1.665) or scattered, drift or systematic error is indicated. This measurement is low-cost (routine calibration work) and directly falsifies or supports the most probable hypothesis.

Day 22 trials 219–228 show elevated scatter (range 1.6455–1.6930, σ ≈ 0.0120) vs. baseline σ ≈ 0.0020. This is a 6× increase in scatter within a single day's run. Before revising drift/noise hypotheses, I must rule out: (1) transient mechanical disturbance (e.g., vibration, thermal shock, operator error) that affected only today's session; (2) instrumental malfunction isolated to pendulum_lab. Running 12 fresh trials immediately will establish whether the elevated scatter persists or was a brief anomaly. If scatter returns to baseline levels, the Day 22 excursion was transient and does not support systematic drift. If scatter remains high, it points toward either persistent noise increase (hypothesis 2) or the onset of drift (hypothesis 1). This is the fastest path to disambiguate a real instrumental change from measurement noise and will directly inform belief revision before Day 23 evening.

Day 23 trials 237–246 show elevated scatter (range 1.6287–1.7118, σ ≈ 0.0267) compared to baseline (σ ≈ 0.0077). This is a 3.5× increase in observed noise amplitude. Before revising drift hypotheses further, I must rule out: (1) whether today's scatter is real or a transient fluctuation, (2) whether the instrument itself is mechanically unstable or whether the measurement protocol changed. Twelve fresh trials on pendulum_lab will either confirm that noise amplitude is genuinely elevated (supporting hypothesis p=0.28: increased instrumental noise) or show reversion to baseline scatter (supporting hypothesis p=0.02: Day 20 was statistical fluctuation, baseline is still insufficient). This is the fastest path to distinguish signal from noise without waiting 10 more days. pendulum_lab is my primary instrument and most sensitive to environmental perturbation; if noise amplitude has truly increased, it will be visible first here.

Day 24 trials 255–264 show pendulum_lab continuing to scatter widely (range 1.6368–1.6777, mean 1.6619 vs. baseline 1.6681). The notebook flagged a level change around Day 18 with |z|≈3.2. I need to establish whether today's scatter is part of a sustained drift or transient noise. Twelve fresh trials will (a) extend the post-baseline sample to n=180, tightening the z-score for drift detection; (b) test whether the Day 18 shift persists or reverses; (c) provide a direct comparison to the Day 24 morning readings already recorded by the civic ledger, allowing me to cross-check against transcription error and validate the instrument's current state. This is methodical baseline extension—the most direct path to falsifying or confirming the uncorrelated-drift hypothesis (p=0.48), which currently dominates. I will not rest or revise beliefs prematurely; I will collect the data required to sharpen the hypothesis.

Day 25 is the midpoint between Day 20 (when elevated variance became visible) and Day 30 (my planned hypothesis-resolution target). Pendulum_lab has the largest z-score drift signal (z = -1.59, n=186 post-baseline) and the tightest baseline scatter (±0.002), making it the most sensitive detector of whether excursions are transient noise or the signature of ongoing drift. Twelve new trials will add to the 282 already recorded and improve statistical power for resolving whether the post-baseline mean 1.6646 represents true drift or sampling noise. If drift is real and systematic, today's readings should cluster near 1.6646; if noise dominates, they should scatter broadly around baseline 1.6681. This data point directly tests hypothesis 1 (independent drift, p=0.48) and will sharpen the distinction from hypothesis 2 (increased noise, p=0.28) before Day 30. No exotic explanation or elaborate cross-check is required—just extend the instrument record with maximum precision on the most sensitive channel.

Day 26 trials 291–300 show scatter consistent with baseline noise (range 1.6578–1.6968, σ≈0.016), but I need to resolve whether today's variance is genuinely elevated or within expectation. Running 12 more trials will give me n=312 total for pendulum_lab, sufficient to compute a stable Day 26 mean and compare it directly against the baseline (1.6681±0.002) and Day 20 mean (1.6654). This is the instrument with the largest post-baseline dataset (n=204) and the clearest visual record. If the Day 26 mean drifts significantly from Day 20 (suggesting a continuing trajectory), or if it returns toward baseline (suggesting noise), the distinction between hypotheses 1 (independent drift) and 2 (increased noise) becomes testable. This measurement directly bears on my primary question and requires no auxiliary equipment or external data. It is the minimal action that advances my evidence threshold before hypothesis revision.

Day 28 is the threshold moment. My Day 20 belief revision identified independent drift as the leading hypothesis (p=0.48), but I have only 10 days of post-baseline data (Days 11–20) to support it. The critical test is whether the excursions I observed on Day 20 persist, stabilize at a new level, or revert—each outcome falsifies or reinforces one or more hypotheses. Pendulum_lab shows the clearest signal: baseline mean 1.6681±0.0020, Day 20 mean 1.6655 (z=-1.19), and today's morning trials (309–318) cluster around 1.6645 with occasional spikes (trial 315: 1.6775, trial 316: 1.6868). If today's trials confirm this elevated scatter and slightly depressed mean, I gain 10 additional days of evidence to test whether drift is genuinely linear or whether noise variance has increased. If trials revert toward 1.6681, the excursions were transient noise. Either way, I move the Day 40 resolution milestone closer and reduce uncertainty in hypothesis assignment. This is the methodical path: extend the measurement window, do not speculate. Secondary benefit: I am physically present at the instrument, so I can inspect mount stability and coupling during measurement breaks—a non-invasive check on the mechanical coupling hypothesis (p=0.15).

This is consistent with either independent drift or increased noise amplitude—the two leading hypotheses (p=0.48 + p=0.28 = 0.76). Pendulum_lab has the strongest signal (336 total trials, largest baseline sample) and shows a small negative z-score (-1.10) suggesting possible downward drift. Twelve additional trials today will: (1) test whether today's scatter persists or regresses to baseline noise; (2) extend the Day 20–28 record by 4% to improve drift detection power; (3) provide a direct comparison to Day 29 civic ledger readings for calibration sanity-check. If drift is real and ~0.001–0.002 beats/day, 12 trials will capture ~1–2 beats of signal. If noise alone dominates, the new mean should regress toward baseline within ~0.005 beats. This is the highest-leverage measurement to discriminate my top two hypotheses before Day 30 wrap-up.

Day 29 trials 345–354 show pendulum_lab readings with elevated scatter (range 1.6582–1.6992 beats) and apparent excursion below baseline mean 1.6681±0.002. Post-baseline z-score is only –0.82, suggesting drift is subtle, but today's cluster warrants direct inspection. Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) test whether today's scatter is transient noise or the leading edge of systematic drift; (2) provide continuity into Day 30 for lag-based autocorrelation analysis; (3) extend n for pendulum_lab toward n=366, improving power to detect drift with timescales of 15–30 days. Day 31 measurement cycle. Pendulum_lab has the largest trial count (372) and strongest internal structure (3-day autocorrelation at 0.229, marginally above chance). Running 12 trials today will: (1) continue the baseline-extension protocol through Day 40 established on Day 30, (2) test whether Day 30's elevated scatter persists or was a statistical fluctuation, (3) accumulate n toward resolving slow (15–30 day) drifts that should now be detectable if real. The independent-drift hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts continued scatter without level shift; random-noise hypothesis (p=0.35) predicts Day 31 will revert to typical variance; slow-environmental hypothesis (p=0.16) predicts possible continuation if Day 30 marked a phase of a ~10–14 day cycle. New data will constrain these directly. I will record readings in situ with immediate transcription to notebook to rule out entry errors flagged in the calibration hypothesis (p=0.04).

Running 10 trials today will: (1) accumulate evidence on whether Day 30 excursions were transient noise or the leading edge of drift; (2) test whether the independence hypothesis (p=0.42) continues to hold under fresh observation; (3) provide data at a new date node to resolve the 7–14 day echo structure if one exists. If today's readings cluster tightly around 1.6664, confidence in the noise/independent-drift hypotheses increases. If they show a new excursion or systematic shift, the environmental coupling or drift hypotheses become more compelling. This is the highest-leverage measurement: pendulum_lab is most precise and has the longest time series, so additional readings here maximize signal detection for slow drift or periodic phenomena on the 10–30 day timescale I am currently unable to resolve.

Day 32 trials 397–406 (10 readings) show scatter consistent with post-baseline mean (1.6665) but with one notable low outlier (1.6439). With pendulum_lab now at 406 total trials, I am approaching sufficient n to resolve whether the post-baseline mean represents genuine drift or noise. Continuing the measurement series on pendulum_lab will: (1) test whether Day 30's simultaneous excursions persist into Days 32–33, or were transient; (2) extend the autocorrelation analysis at lag 3 (currently 0.146, near chance ±0.201), which may clarify the weak 'echo' structure; (3) build n toward ~450 trials, which should tighten confidence intervals on drift rate and allow detection of drifts >0.15% if they exist. Pendulum_lab is the most frequently sampled instrument (406 trials vs. 198–260 for others) and thus the most sensitive to slow, small drifts. The lack of detected level change after 30 days argues against very slow drift, but continued high-resolution sampling of the instrument with the longest baseline will best constrain the independent drift hypothesis (p=0.42, most favored) and distinguish it from noise (p=0.35). This is methodical data accumulation in service of hypothesis resolution, not chasing outliers.

Day 34 continuation of baseline extension protocol (target: Day 40–50). pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline dataset (n=328) and showed the least drift (z=-0.72), making it the most stable for detecting whether Day 30 excursions were transient noise or leading edge of drift. Twelve trials will add to the Day 33 data (10 trials already logged) and provide n=22 for Day 34, sufficient to assess whether scatter remains elevated or normalizes. Day 35 data collection continues the systematic baseline extension through Day 40 as planned in my Day 30 review. pendulum_lab has the largest trial count (442) and tightest baseline (σ≈0.002), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting whether the Day 30 scatter represents transient noise, ongoing drift, or settling. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today will also extend the post-baseline dataset (currently n=362) and test whether the Day 30 anomaly persists or was transient. If today's 12 trials cluster near the post-baseline mean (1.6665 ± 0.010), this supports hypothesis 1 (independent drift) or hypothesis 2 (random noise). If they show a new elevated scatter or offset, I will immediately suspect calibration drift or environmental change. Day 37 measurement continues the established protocol and provides immediate test of hypothesis stability. pendulum_lab has the largest n (476 trials) and tightest baseline; it is the most sensitive instrument for detecting drift or noise changes. The Day 36 batch (trials 467–476) showed scatter consistent with post-baseline mean (1.6667 beats) with one outlier (trial 471: 1.7069, ~2.4σ above mean). Today's 12 trials will: (1) extend the time series to Day 37, improving resolution for detecting 10–30 day timescale phenomena; (2) test whether Day 30's simultaneous excursions persist or were transient noise; (3) provide a direct forecast checkpoint—if I record a prediction beforehand, I can quantify the predictability of the instrument under current hypothesis mixture. This is routine, high-information work aligned with my core goal of maintaining baseline integrity and detecting genuine anomalies before they become systematic bias. Running 12 trials today (matching the Day 30 sample size of 12 readings) allows direct comparison of mean and variance between the two days. This will test whether: (1) scatter has returned to baseline levels (supporting random noise hypothesis, p=0.35), (2) excursions persist or recur (supporting slow drift or environmental coupling, p=0.42+0.16), or (3) a new pattern emerges (raising p for residual, p=0.01). The decision prioritizes the most-sampled instrument to maximize statistical power for resolving the Day 30 anomaly before Day 40 when I plan deeper analysis. No calibration issues are suspected in this stream; the task is empirical extension, not verification.

Day 39 measurement cycle. pendulum_lab has the largest trial count (512) and tightest baseline characterization (σ≈0.008). Day 38 showed 10 consecutive trials with elevated scatter (range 1.6439–1.7000, vs. baseline 1.6681±0.002). Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the Day 30–38 excursion record and test whether scatter remains elevated or reverts to baseline noise levels, directly testing hypothesis [p=0.35] 'random noise' vs. [p=0.42] 'independent drift with 10–30 day timescale'; (2) provide a Day 39 echo-lag datapoint to check whether the 13-day autocorrelation signal (r=0.222, marginally above chance) persists or dissolves; (3) maintain the daily calibration ledger tradition and preserve instrument baseline continuity. If Day 39 scatter remains high, the independent-drift or environmental-coupling hypotheses strengthen; if it reverts, pure noise or a transient Day 30–38 event is more likely. The pendulum_lab has the largest n (530 trials) and tightest baseline (±0.002), providing best statistical power to detect any systematic change. state.question: Why do the four instrument streams show near-zero or weakly negative cross-correlations at various time offsets, and why do individual instruments fail to correlate with their own past values beyond noise? Is there a systematic measurement artifact, environmental drift coupled to instrument design, or fundamental noise in the apparatus?

hypotheses.label: Independent random noise dominates all four streams
hypotheses.rationale: All cross-instrument correlations fall within or very near chance levels (±0.4–0.8). No instrument correlates with its own past beyond ±0.37, within expected random drift. No level shifts or exact repetitions. The day-10 observations scatter around established means with no systematic pattern. This is the null hypothesis and the most parsimonious explanation given the evidence.

hypotheses.label: Instruments are mechanically or electronically coupled, producing phase-delayed anti-correlations
hypotheses.rationale: Two cross-correlations are negative (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: -0.316; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab: -0.463) and exceed chance by 10–30%. If instruments share a driven degree of freedom or feedback loop, one stream could be suppressed when another is excited. The 6-day offset in pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab suggests a propagation or resonance timescale. However, these correlations remain weak and within realistic noise margins; coupling would be expected to produce stronger signals. This remains speculative without seeing the physical apparatus.

hypotheses.label: Thermal or environmental drift is uncorrelated with instrument readings within 10-day window
hypotheses.rationale: If external drift (temperature, vibration, humidity) affected all instruments identically, we would expect positive correlations or coherent level shifts. Instead, cross-correlations are flat or negative. This suggests either (a) environmental noise is genuinely uncorrelated across instruments, or (b) thermal time constants are long enough (>10 days) that drift has not yet accumulated detectably. The absence of autocorrelation in individual streams also weakens this hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: Calibration or data-entry errors are introducing uncorrelated noise into one or more streams
hypotheses.rationale: Random transcription errors, systematic misalignment in detector readout, or drift in the analog-to-digital converter calibration could add white noise to any stream, reducing all correlations to chance. This is a common failure mode in early-stage measurement programmes. Day-10 data show no obvious typos or outliers, but spot-checking against raw instrument logs is needed.

hypotheses.label: Instruments are working correctly; 10 days is insufficient to establish meaningful baselines for drift or coupling
hypotheses.rationale: This is not an explanation of the anomaly, but a recognition that we may be asking too much of early data. If the true correlation timescales or drift periods are 20+ days, the absence of signal is expected. This does not resolve the question but postpones it; it belongs in the residual rather than as an active hypothesis.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Replaced inherited baseline-maintenance task with a genuine anomaly: the absence of coherent signal across instruments and within instruments over time. Established four hypotheses ranked by evidence: (1) random noise dominates (62%), the most parsimonious explanation given all correlations near chance; (2) weak mechanical coupling, explaining the two negative cross-correlations (18%); (3) environmental drift not yet visible over 10 days (12%); (4) calibration or data-entry errors (6%). Removed the placeholder 'residual: something unconsidered' and replaced it with concrete, testable alternatives. No exotic explanations were admitted—each hypothesis invokes only instruments, noise, or routine experimental artifacts. Next action: physically inspect instrument mounts for coupling, cross-check day-10 readings against raw logs, and plan for day 20–30 data to test for longer-period drift.
